'On the Road'

The world is wide as well as long,
And it’s open to our longing--
But what we want must be enough,
Or else there’s no good rough-hewing!

I see an infant child playing joyfully
He finds a dead bird on the doorstep, laughter fills his face
When he shows it to her mother, sorrow comes flooding in
She clutches the child and cries bitterly

author: emily_dickinson
text:
For me to write, as I am writing it,
 All is not done;
 To read and think and try to do what has been written,
 And then again to write for more than twice
 What has already been given—all this is pleasure.

 The great thing would be to say it once well.

Faroese is spoken by approximately 50,000 people on the Faroe Islands (Denmark) and around 25,014 worldwide. It has no known historical relation to any other language or languages. Faroese does have some similarities with Icelandic and Old Norse: Faroese was originally written in an early version of Gothic script that shares many features with Anglo-Saxon runes, but it then shifted into Latin characters, which are still used today. It also resembles Norwegian and Swedish, due to its geographical position between them.

author: cushag
text:
As Johnny and me were married many years ago,
We have a goodly number of children who are now grown up;
"Mayry, mayry, ma-a-a -ay," says one,
And "Johnny, johnny, john-o-ohn-ee," cries another.

Well, this makes my days pass quickly as they fill me with care
For all that I can do is to wash dishes or keep house
While Johnny runs off again for more meat.I often wish he would behave like a man!

author: emily_dickinson
text: This is not a love poem but an elegy for a beloved one who has died. The speaker tells us that he or she has only this body with him/her, and then offers his heart as well, which makes the situation even more sad. In the next line we learn that there are many things that belong to the person referred to by the speaker: "all the meadows, wide" (line 4). The word meadow can mean different kinds of spaces such as a field or a yard. Here it seems to refer to some kind of open space where flowers grow and animals live.

author: john_keats
text: The sun sets on the horizon and casts its last rays upon the earth. The shadows grow long as twilight descends, painting the sky in hues of orange and pink. A lone man walks down a gravel path, his eyes fixed on a distant castle nestled atop a hill. As he approaches, the silhouette of the towering structure becomes clearer against the fading sunlight. Finally reaching the entrance, the door creaks open as he enters, casting an eerie glow throughout the darkened interior. He follows winding staircases deep into the heart of the ancient fortress, exploring hidden chambers filled with crumbling furniture and dusty books.

I have been reading a lot lately, and I keep getting ideas from it.
So here is my first shot at a form-poem:

There was once a time when life
was simple and pure
but now we live in a world
full of strife
with pain and hurt
and tears to spare
when love is lost
we lose our care.

author: stothert_james_a
text:
The wind, the winter’s fury,

Brought its blasts upon that shore ;

And the pale moon overhung it,

Looking out upon her sorrow.

Yak-siyuk, yak-siya-yik! (Yak-saeuck)
The little birds fly out from their nest,
From the trees and bushes they are flying away.

They’re singing so loud
To wake up all the nature around !
Let them not be afraid –
Their nests will never leave us for a day.

We’ll protect them
In every way we can,
So that they could live long life
And bring happiness to our land...

I know a place where there is no night,

For all its sun, that evermore burns high ;

No darkness shadows it with shadow, nor light

Ever so fierce to make it hot or dry.

There are not here these things which man loves best :

Love's soft caresses and his pleasures rare,

And every joy which men have learned to prize,

All save one joy which never comes there.

And there is nothing more to be said;
They come out as one man from his quiver,
And they shoot them down into the sky;

Or like the smoke that goes before the wind—
For the light comes and then we look at it!

Tswana traditional poetry can be divided into three genres namely:
•    Song, which includes praise poems and work songs (e.g. hunting song).
•     Narrative or story telling.  These are usually about legendary heroes like Mosoeu Kgafela and King Mogae I, who were responsible for the creation of Tswana society and culture. 
•      Religious or spiritual themes that include prayers to the spirits of the ancestors.

author: william_wordsworth
text:
My country’s morning sun shines like a beacon,
As bright as stars, guiding me through each dawn.
It fills our hearts with joy and stirs our souls,
With its warmth and light, inspiring us to explore.
Our nation stands tall, proud and resolute,
A force to reckon with, forever undefeated.
We may face storms and trials along the way,
But together we stand strong, united by day.

author: william_wordsworth
text:
O Earthly Star, Shine upon us with your light,
 As we stand together side by side.
 Your beams will guide our way, so bright they shine,
 And never dim from those whose souls are kind.
 We rise up strong against all opposition,
 With hearts united, for this nation's sake.
 May every man feel what he believes within,
 For only then can we truly make amends.
